extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, scholars of law and church-state relations, and lawmakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of normative criteria for distinguishing ecclesiastical (spiritual) and civil (temporal) powers, what counts as a law versus counsel, and when obedience or jurisdiction properly belongs to civil sovereigns or church authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Law and Counsell
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason of a Law is taken from the design and benefit of him that prescribeth it; the reason of a Counsell is from the design and benefit of him to whom the Counsell is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws are authoritative commands grounded in the prescriber's authority and aim at the prescriber's design; Counsels aim at the recipient's good and are conditional (e.g., 'if they to whom they give it, will attain their ends'). Example: abstaining from strangled things and blood is a burden given as counsel, not an absolute law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic acts as Counsels not Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of the Apostles and their councils aimed only at the benefit (salvation) of converted Gentiles and therefore are Counsels rather than Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Apostles sought the salvation of others and would receive reward regardless of obedience, their decrees are counsel-like rather than legislative commands enforceable by temporal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'higher powers' (Rom. 13) limited to civil sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Let every soul be subject to the higher powers' is meant of secular, not of separate ecclesiastical princes; ecclesiastical princes are only such as are also civil sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where bishops are not civil sovereigns they lack temporal jurisdiction; Christ's teaching about serving two masters makes impossible a separate and equal temporal authority in the Pope apart from civil sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication is not a temporal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apostle's power (e.g., to 'use sharpness') is not to inflict temporal punishments (death, imprisonment, fines) but to excommunicate — a social exclusion rather than a civil punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excommunication 'is no more but a leaving of their company' and can be more painful for the one excommunicated than for the excommunicant; it denotes spiritual/social sanction, not civil coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Rod' (1 Cor. 4.21) denotes ecclesiastical censure not magistrate punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Shall I come unto you with a Rod, or in love…' — the 'rod' here refers to excommunication or denouncing of punishment to be inflicted by Christ at Judgment, not to a magistrate's temporal power to punish now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'rod' is a sign of spiritual discipline and future divine revenge upon enemies, not authorization for bishops to exercise civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescriptive precepts to disciples are counsel not law
rubrics_metrics.description: Precepts given to disciples (e.g., Timothy 3.2 on bishops' qualifications) are advice to a disciple/teacher relationship, not legislative commands binding as laws in a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Timothy was a disciple and his flock his scholars, directives to him (e.g., 'Drink no longer water, but use a little wine') are counsel; only an absolute subjection to a person converts a precept into a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedural precepts (1 Tim. 5.19) are wise counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules like 'Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses' are wise precepts but not laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They function as prudential guidance for good order rather than as enforceable legislative commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing apostles tied to lawful ordination, not automatic legislative force (Luke 10.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He that heareth you, heareth me' applies to those ordained pastors by lawful authority; even so, a Christian king's teaching, as pastor, does not of itself become law or bind belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign Christian may authorize laws consistent with doctrine, but cannot compel internal belief; external obedience commanded by a sovereign is action-based and separable from inward conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Obey' in apostolic epistles often means hearkening/practice, not legal obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek terms translated 'obey' (e.g., upakouei) can mean 'hearkening to' or 'putting in practice' advice as well as obeying a punishing authority; thus epistolary admonitions imply reputation-based social sanctions, not civil punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When apostles say 'obey' they do not ordain capital or corporal penalties; they recommend avoidance of company or public shame as corrective measures rather than legal coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to pastors (Heb. 13.17) is for benefit of souls, not legislative submission
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obey your leaders… for they watch for your souls' indicates obedience as following counsel toward salvation, not as submitting to a pastor's legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If everything taught by pastors were law, every parish pastor would have legislative power. Additionally, believers are commanded to 'try the spirits' (1 John 4.1), showing doctrinal dispute is permitted and inconsistent with absolute legal commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction defined as power to hear, determine causes, prescribe rules, and enforce them
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction is the power of hearing and determining causes between man and man, prescribing rules of right and wrong, and compelling obedience (with the sword of justice) — capacities belonging only to civil sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishops who lack powers to make and enforce laws in the temporal order have no jurisdiction in the proper sense; where a bishop holds civil sovereignty he may have jurisdiction by virtue of that sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops' jurisdiction derives from civil sovereigns unless pope holds civil sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishops receive authority from the civil sovereign of the place; they do not universally hold jurisdiction De Jure Divino apart from such mediation (except where the Pope is also civil sovereign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments from scriptural gifts (Eph. 4.11) show spiritual office but do not prove immediate divine grant of jurisdiction independent of civil polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchical derivation of authority favors civil sovereign primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because monarchy concentrates authority in one man from whom others derive, church government described as 'monarchicall' actually supports civil monarchs as real monarchs of their people's church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all authority derives by derivation from one sovereign in a monarchy, then the civil sovereign will be source of jurisdiction within his dominion; this undermines claims of independent papal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality of ecclesiastical jurisdictions indicates human, not divine, origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in the size and extent of bishops' jurisdictions (town vs province) show these differences are set by human rulers (princes) not by divine command; hence ecclesiastical jurisdiction is of human, not immediate divine, origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If jurisdiction were immediately divine, equality in jurisdiction would follow; observed inequality supports derivation from civil structures and princes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal temporal power cannot be inferred from pastoral (spiritual) authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that spiritual supremacy entails the right to dispose of temporal powers (depose princes, transfer kingdoms) is invalid; spiritual authority being subordinate or instrumental to temporal government does not confer coercive temporal jurisdiction over sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction of temporal and spiritual can only mean means-to-end relations, not person-level subjection; to infer papal temporal supremacy from pastoral power conflates categories and misapplies 'subjection'.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 'spiritual commonwealth' on earth to lawfully depose temporal sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no earthly spiritual commonwealth distinct from civil commonwealth; the kingdom of Christ is 'not of this world' and will be established at the Resurrection, so no present spiritual sovereign may lawfully wield temporal coercion over states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a terrestrial spiritual sovereign representing all Christendom, claims that the Pope may depose princes for spiritual reasons lack foundation, except where the Pope also possesses civil sovereignty by consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjection of persons cannot be inferred from subordination of arts or ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if civil government is ordered toward spiritual ends, that subordination of ends does not imply personal subjection of the civil sovereign to the spiritual; 'one Power may be subordinate to another, as the art of a Sadler to the art of a Rider' but persons remain distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category error: rights, subjection, command attach to persons, not to abstract 'powers' — therefore pastoral aims do not create a personal duty of obedience of the sovereign to the Pope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of heresy and toleration belongs to civil sovereigns in public matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment whether a king's teaching is heresy in the public sense belongs to the civil sovereign because 'haeresie is… a private opinion, obstinately maintained, contrary to the opinion which the publique person… hath commanded to be taught.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects tolerating a prince's public teaching and failing to depose him is a matter of conscience and faith obligations; but deposing a chosen prince for opinion alone violates the law of nature and faith (violates promise to obey) unless previously determined by rightful process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptismal promises by kings do not subordinate them to papal coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Although kings baptised promise to defend Christian faith, this submission does not make them papal fellows or place them under papal coercive authority; they remain supreme pastors of their own subjects where they are sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A king's pastoral role in his dominion is compatible with his civil supremacy; promises made in baptism are not a legal instrument to transfer temporal jurisdiction to the Pope.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Feed my sheep' grants teaching power, not coercive power over princes
rubrics_metrics.description: Command to 'Feed my sheep' confers pastoral authority to teach and care for souls but does not, in Scripture, authorize pastors to depose or kill kings or otherwise exercise temporal coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural admonitions (e.g., beware false prophets) were given as counsel to multitudes; they counsel avoidance and warning, not violent or coercive action against rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical examples do not prove rightful authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of bishops or popes deposing rulers (e.g., Ambrose and Theodosius; papal depositions) do not establish legitimacy of papal temporal power; examples may be crimes or acts in the pope's own cause and are not legal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on precedent alone is insufficient; examples must be judged by law and justice rather than taken as proof of right.

rubrics_metrics.name: When commands of God and man conflict, one must obey God if known to be God's command
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person receives two contrary commands and knows that one is from God, he ought to obey God and not the other, even if the other come from a lawful sovereign or father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real difficulty arises in cases of uncertainty — when a man cannot tell whether the command is truly divine or whether God's name is being misused by a person pursuing private ends; resolving that epistemic uncertainty is the frequent pretext for sedition and civil war.
